figures.label: S2
figures.caption: Figure S2. Schematic illustration of depth profiling experiment. Data were collected on a cylindrical battery stack in which the beam height (20 microns) was small relative to the height of the cathode (172 microns) and the anode (250 microns). During experiments, the sample was translated vertically with a 20 microns step size so that the beam would probe different heights within the cathode film, with a series of consecutive patterns for regions of the cell shown here in a waterfall plot. As a result, diffraction patterns from the cathode (indicated with red dashed lines) could be collected free of signals from the anode, with only partial overlap from the signal from the stainless steel pills (iron peaks marked with black arrows). A signal from the Teflon cell housing (green) was seen at all heights.

figures.caption: Figure S3. Extra broadening of diffraction peaks on the 2D area detector due to the extended length of the sample along the path of the beam. Ideally, a point sample at a distance D from the 2D area detector that is normal to the beam path produces a diffraction spot that is measured at a radius R from the spot where the beam intersects the detector. If the sample is extended along the beam path away from the detector to have a finite pathlength of L along the beam, diffraction will occur at the same angle 2θ from both the front and back of the sample (dashed lines) as well as all points in between. The measured reflection on the detector will therefore also be extended by a width W, which will be approximately equal to L sin 2θ at low angles where the approximate relationship sin(2θ) ≈ 2θ holds when the diffraction angle is specified in radians. figures.label: S5
figures.caption: Figure S5. Influence of tilt misalignment on depth-profiling diffraction data, with the aspect ratio and tilt of the sample (grey rectangle) drawn approximately to scale. The tilt of the sample during experiments was estimated to be about 2.9° for the sample cycled at C/10 and 2.4° for the sample cycled at C/3 (fits shown in Figure S6). Due to the aspect ratio of this sample (172 microns thick, 4750 microns wide), this misalignment results in an X-ray beam passing through the sample center (green) interrogating all heights of the sample. However, when the beam is translated ~150 microns above (red) or below (violet), it is still possible to exclusively probe the top (front) or bottom (back) of the cathode film. The beam passes through a significantly reduced volume when it is moved away from the sample center, resulting in a reduced intensity away from the center position (Figure S6).
